overview: Medieval Corsica was a mountainous island of villages, local lords and ports connected to Italy. Pisa and Genoa competed for influence, while island communities and powerful families pursued their own interests. The map colours the whole island as one unit, but this is a regional history: no single independent Corsican state governed it continuously from 1000 to 1492.

periods.title: Maritime rivals and local powers
periods.summary: Pisan and Genoese influence developed alongside island lordships and communities.

periods.title: San Giorgio and contested government
periods.summary: Genoa entrusted the island to the Office of Saint George; authority remained contested.

items.text: In 1133, the pope divided jurisdiction over Corsica’s six bishoprics between Pisa and Genoa. Church appointments were part of the competition for influence. Genoese capture and settlement at Bonifacio in the late twelfth century also gave that maritime republic a strong coastal foothold.

Thirteenth-century Bonifacio connected southern Corsica, Sardinia and Liguria. Ships carried hides, cheese and salted foods toward the Ligurian coast, and brought back cloth and pottery. These connections put overseas goods within reach of island ports long before modern ferries.

Calvi exported wine and cereals from the Balagne district. Coastal trading towns did not automatically govern all the surrounding countryside: much of the island remained rural, and local opposition repeatedly limited Genoese control.

The agreement of 1453 with the Office of Saint George specified a tax of twenty Genoese soldi per hearth, a household taxation unit. The amount did not vary with wealth. A small-looking fixed bill could therefore weigh very differently on rich and poor households.

Under that agreement, much civil justice remained local, within a district called a pieve. Officials and judges came from the neighbourhood. Criminal cases and appeals were exceptions, so settling a dispute close to home did not mean complete independence from higher authorities.

Excavations at Cotone near Bastia reveal a settlement abandoned around the middle of the fourteenth century. Several dozen houses occupied a rocky height above the plain, protected by walls and a small castle. The village’s position combined a wide view with a steep walk home.

Cotone’s carefully built dry-stone houses mostly exceeded fifty square metres. The excavator thought they generally had an upper floor. Rooms often had separate outside entrances, while a small vaulted oven in one room probably served for heating or cooking. The evidence preserves a working home, not its recipe book.

More than half the pottery fragments recovered at Cotone came from a group including green-and-brown decorated jugs, small amphoras and plain red pitchers attributed to Ligurian and Pisan workshops. Local cooking pots also appeared. Broken crockery lets archaeologists connect a mountain village’s tables and kitchens with Mediterranean trade.

At Bonifacio, the municipality built a cistern beneath the porch of Sainte-Marie-Majeure in the thirteenth century. It collected rain from the church and neighbouring roofs and could hold about 650 cubic metres. Water was drawn through openings in the porch’s broad pillars: a church entrance also helped keep the town supplied.

The Franciscans were established at Bonifacio by the late thirteenth century, outside the town walls. Their convent stood among vegetation including wild olives and junipers. Religious communities needed buildings and land for daily work as well as places for prayer.

A well built in 1398 by the master mason Abrigho de Pistoïa supplied the Franciscan community and watered its vegetable and fruit garden. A surviving piece of water engineering brings us closer to the friars’ ordinary chores: drawing water, tending plants and keeping meals possible.

sections.title: A person in the written record

items.text: The 1453 oath list preserves the Latinised name “Franciosus de Murato”, meaning “Franciosus from Murato”, as transcribed by linguist Jean Chiorboli. People were often identified by a personal name and home locality; some entries added a father’s name to avoid confusion. This is administrative Latin, not a recording of everyday Corsican speech.

Ajaccio’s foundation in 1492 belonged to a wider Genoese effort to reorganise the island around coastal centres. This process could be harsh: it accompanied the destruction of lordly strongholds and the depopulation of some southern districts. Building a new port could transform the lives of people far beyond its walls.

ending.text: The imported record stops in 1492, when Corsican society was being reorganised rather than disappearing. Genoese government continued beyond that date. In 1562 the Republic established a new Corsican magistracy after the Office of Saint George returned the island to direct republican administration.
